title: Guru Hargobind's gurpurab
hookLine: remembered with the two swords of miri and piri

lines: A BOY WHO HAS LOST HIS FATHER.
cards: A boy, about eleven by tradition's count, has just lost his father. Not to an accident.

Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, the man who built the Harmandir Sahib and gathered the Granth, has died in custody in Lahore; Sikhs remember it as his shaheedi, his martyrdom. The Sikhs are grieving and afraid.
And when the boy becomes the sixth Guru, he does something new. Tradition says he asks for two swords, and he puts on both. Today: Akal Takht.

teach.b: Guru Hargobind was born near Amritsar. You've met his birth already: the shabad of Guru Arjan's joy when his son arrived.
After his father's execution he became Guru, and the two swords he wore became a lasting idea in Sikh life. One sword was miri: worldly power, responsibility in the world, the duty to protect.
The other was piri: spiritual authority, the life of devotion and the Name. The words echo two titles: mir, a ruler, and pir, a spiritual guide. The point wasn't two separate lives.
A Sikh holds both at once. As Sikhs often explain it, devotion without courage can abandon the weak, and power without devotion turns cruel.
The two swords keep each other honest. He gave the idea a building.

teach.h: THE AKAL TAKHT FACES THE HARMANDIR.
teach.b: Facing the Harmandir Sahib, he raised a platform called the Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One. The Harmandir is where the Word is sung; the Akal Takht is where the community gathers to decide, and act.
Even today, they stand looking at each other across the same courtyard. Guru Hargobind kept horses and armed followers, and fought battles with Mughal forces.
He was also, tradition remembers, a man of deep devotion who kept the kirtan going morning and evening.
The two outer swords of the Khanda emblem are often read the same way. His gurpurab is marked with kirtan, and in some places with displays of gatka, the Sikh martial art. Two swords, one Guru.

how: On Guru Hargobind's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and some communities display gatka; Sikhs remember his two swords of miri and piri and the Akal Takht he founded.

o: the throne of the Timeless One
the golden temple in the pool
the sword worn for worldly power

games.q: the sixth Guru — tap the pairs.
p: the throne of the Timeless One

s: miri and piri mean living two separate lives
they mean holding duty and devotion at once, each keeping the other honest.
the Akal Takht faces the Harmandir Sahib
they stand across the same courtyard: the Word sung, and the community deciding.

games.q: you're a boy, your father has been martyred, and you're the new Guru. what does Guru Hargobind do?
o: put on two swords, miri and piri.
stop the kirtan until it's safe.
games.why: he wore two swords, worldly duty and spiritual authority, and founded the Akal Takht facing the Harmandir.

practice: If you can, stand, feet planted, shoulders back, chin level; if you can't, sit as tall as you can.

Feel your weight evenly on both sides, one for your duties in the world, one for your inner life, and breathe in strength, breathe out stillness. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing like that.

wordCard.voice: Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One Guru Hargobind raised facing the Harmandir Sahib, where the community gathers to decide and act.

orig.note: Punjabi: worldly and spiritual authority, from the titles mir, ruler, and pir, guide.

carryVoice: Your line: two swords. Courage and devotion, each one worn every day. See you tomorrow.
